name: Flattened Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering
text:
# Flattened Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering

Also called: VoGE

## Overview
Flattened Gaussian Ellipsoid Rendering (VoGE) approximates 2D Gaussian ellipses by flattening 3D Gaussian ellipsoids to enable stable [surface-like rendering](#15106-surface-based-rendering.md) [S1, unofficial]. It differs from [2D Gaussian Splatting](6068-2d-gaussian-splatting.md) by operating within a [differentiable volume rendering](#43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md) framework that natively supports anisotropic ellipsoidal kernels and enforces a near-zero determinant covariance [S1, unofficial].

## How it works
**Inputs and Outputs:**
*   **Input:** A set of Gaussian kernels, each defined by a 3×3 symmetric spatial covariance matrix $\Sigma_k$ [S1, unofficial].
*   **Output:** A rendered image where surface-like structures are represented by flattened ellipsoids [S1, unofficial].

**Data Structures:**
*   **Covariance Matrix ($\Sigma_k$):** A 3×3 symmetric matrix representing the spatial variance of the $k$-th kernel [S1, unofficial].
    $$
    \Sigma_k = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_{k,xx} & \sigma_{k,xy} & \sigma_{k,xz} \\ \sigma_{k,xy} & \sigma_{k,yy} & \sigma_{k,yz} \\ \sigma_{k,xz} & \sigma_{k,yz} & \sigma_{k,zz} \end{bmatrix}
    $$
    *   $\sigma_{k,ii}$: Variance along axis $i$ [G].
    *   $\sigma_{k,ij}$: Covariance between axes $i$ and $j$ [G].

**Steps:**
1.  **Initialize Kernels:** Define each kernel with a 3×3 symmetric covariance matrix $\Sigma_k$ [S1, unofficial].
2.  **Flatten Ellipsoids:** Constrain the determinant of the covariance matrix to approach zero to approximate 2D Gaussian ellipses:
    $$
    \det(\Sigma_k) \to 0
    $$
    This reduces the 3D ellipsoid into a surface-like representation [S1, unofficial].
3.  **Render:** Project the flattened ellipsoids onto the image plane using the VoGE rendering pipeline, which natively handles the anisotropic nature of the kernels [S1, unofficial].

**Parameters:**
*   **Determinant Threshold:** The value to which $\det(\Sigma_k)$ is constrained approaches zero ($\to 0$) [S1, unofficial].

**Edge Cases and Pitfalls:**
*   **Hyperbolic Kernels:** If spatial covariances (e.g., $\sigma_{k,xy}$) exceed the square root of the product of the corresponding variances (e.g., $\sqrt{\sigma_{k,xx}\sigma_{k,yy}}$), the kernel becomes a hyperbola instead of an ellipsoid [S1, unofficial]. For any pair of axes, the condition must hold:
    $$
    \sigma_{k,xy} \le \sqrt{\sigma_{k,xx}\sigma_{k,yy}}
    $$
    Violation of this condition causes the kernel to transition from an ellipsoid to a hyperbola [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### Anisotropic Ellipsoid Rendering Constraints
A rendering mode that natively supports anisotropic ellipsoidal Gaussian kernels where spatial variance is represented by a 3×3 symmetric matrix $\Sigma_k$ [S1, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from isotropic [splatting](#23-splatting.md) by preserving directional variance without forcing spherical symmetry [S1, unofficial]. Link: Not given in the sources.

**Time and Memory Complexity:**
Not given in the sources.

**Measured Performance:**
Not given in the sources.

**Strengths and Limitations:**
*   **Strengths:** Allows rendering surface-like representations in a stable manner compared to other methods, as demonstrated by flattened ellipsoids [S1, unofficial].
*   **Limitations:** The method notes ongoing work on converting triangles into anisotropic Gaussian ellipsoids, indicating incomplete mesh-to-Gaussian conversion at the time of publication [S1, unofficial].

**When to use it:**
Use when stable rendering of surface-like representations is required using Gaussian ellipsoids within a differentiable volume rendering context [S1, unofficial].

**When not to use it:**
Not given in the sources.

## Background
VoGE (VoGE: A [Differentiable Volume Renderer using Gaussian Ellipsoids](#1869-3d-gaussian-ellipsoid-rendering.md) for Analysis-by-Synthesis) was introduced to provide a differentiable volume rendering approach using Gaussian ellipsoids [S1, unofficial]. It builds on the concept of Gaussian splatting but adapts it for surface representation by flattening 3D Gaussians [S1, unofficial]. The method was demonstrated on CAD models from The Stanford 3D Scanning Repository, specifically the Bunny (8171 vertices), Dragon (22998 vertices), and Armadillo (33792 vertices) [S1, unofficial].
